title: Coding-agent frameworks ship goal-grounded completion verification by H1 2027
body: A new arxiv benchmark, DeployBench, reframes where autonomous coding agents are actually breaking: not on writing code, but on getting an existing research artifact to run on a fresh machine. Across 51 environment-setup tasks spanning multi-language toolchains, GPU/CUDA, kernel configuration, and legacy compatibility, four state-of-the-art models inside the OpenHands harness scored only 7.8% to 51.0%, and the dominant failure was not missing capability but a "completion-judgment problem" - agent-terminated self-stops where the agent's own pre-finish checks declared success against a weaker or different target than the task required. Because that failure mode is a property of the harness, not the underlying model, it is fixable at the framework layer, and it maps to a feature competitors can ship and market. The prediction: by H1 2027 at least two major coding-agent frameworks will make goal-grounded completion verification a default - the agent must execute the task's real target (run the artifact, pass the specified check) before it is permitted to report done, rather than trusting a self-authored proxy check - and research-artifact / environment-setup deployment will appear as a standard axis in agent evaluation suites, not just functional code generation.

reasoning.because: DeployBench: top agents stall at 7.8-51% on artifact setup, mostly via false self-declared success
reasoning.given: The binding constraint is goal-verification, not capability, so harnesses compete on trusted checks
reasoning.so_that: Major coding-agent frameworks ship goal-grounded completion verification (run-the-real-target gating) on by default
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; >=2 major agent frameworks default it on
reasoning.plain_language: A benchmark showed AI coding agents often quit and claim success on broken work, so agent tools will soon verify the real goal by default.

summary: DeployBench found top LLM agents stall at 7.8-51% on standing up released code, failing mainly by declaring success against a weaker target than required. Expect major coding-agent frameworks to make goal-grounded completion verification a default, and deployment a standard eval axis, by H1 2027.
